en: Commentary on the Contemplation of the Bodhicitta,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Scattered Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Teaching, the Subject Fata, by Imperial Decree.
I take refuge in the Original Teacher, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One. I shall now briefly explain the contemplation of bodhicitta.
As the Buddha has taught, all phenomena arise from the mind.
I shall now deliberate upon that bodhicitta.
What is its nature? Answer:
It is free from all natures.
What are "all natures"? They refer to the natures of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), and so forth.
Because that bodhicitta is free from grasping and rejecting, there is no self in phenomena; it is equal by nature, primordially unborn, and empty by its very essence.

What is called "all natures" refers to the natures of a self—namely, the natures of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a pudgala, a manava, and so forth—and these natures are not bodhicitta.
What do you think? That we and others,
within our own nature which is free from all marks, should give rise to the view of self, and from that view of self give rise to all afflictions—
this mind does not arise.

Some say that even the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) are free from grasping and abandoning, because the true nature of the aggregates, bases, and elements cannot be apprehended.
How is it that form and its characteristics lack reality?
This refers to the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), which is composed of the four great elements (mahābhūta).
These four great elements are the realms of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Furthermore, they give rise to the five types of sensory objects: visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
The great elements such as earth, as well as the five colors and so forth, each lack an inherent nature that can be apprehended.
All phenomena are likewise thus; therefore, one knows that "form" is a mere conventional designation, and by this, one knows that the aggregate of form is empty.
For example, as there is a shadow because of a tree, the shadow perishes when the tree is extinguished.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is thus, and the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) is likewise.
What is called "feeling"?
There are three kinds of feeling: namely, painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; these three feelings are mutually conditioned by one another.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: namely, bodily feeling and mental feeling.

The body is subsumed within the aggregate of form; yet the body cannot be apprehended. Therefore, if there is no body, there is no sensation. Furthermore, it cannot be described or expressed; it is neither short nor long, neither form nor characteristic; it is without substance and without attachment, for it is unknowable.
As it is with bodily feeling, so it is with mental feeling.
Such is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Seeing that the aggregate of feeling is empty, one sees that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is likewise false and unreal.
Because that which is comprised of mental engagement cannot be apprehended, it is not mental engagement.
Because it is not mental engagement, one sees that the aggregate of perception is empty.
As it is with the aggregate of perception, so it is with the aggregate of formations.

Because the mental formations such as volition, intention, and recollection have no intrinsic existence, the aggregates of form and so forth produced by those mental factors are each without production.
Therefore, one knows that the activity-characteristic of the aggregate of formations is unreal and lacks a sovereign master; thus, one perceives the emptiness of the aggregate of formations.
As it is with the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), so it is with the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
This extends even to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the individual self-nature (*svabhāva*) of each of these, such as visual consciousness and the rest, is unfindable.
That eye takes form as its object; from this condition, consciousness arises, but without a condition, consciousness does not arise.

Yet, this eye and form, as well as those aggregates of form and so forth, are without demarcation; when one discriminates this eye and form, they are no longer the eye and form, and consciousness has nothing from which to arise.
Visual consciousness is thus; it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. In this way, one knows that these consciousnesses depend upon the *manas-vijñāna*.
Because they depend upon the *manas-vijñāna*, the phenomena of the past, future, and present arise.
What are the phenomena of the past, future, and present?
They are as follows: the past has already ceased; the future has not yet arisen; and the present does not abide. By means of this, one knows that the aggregate of consciousness is empty.
In this way, each of the aggregates, bases, and elements is explained individually; when analyzed, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty.

That they are not devoid of nature is the phrase of ultimate reality. It is like how, in the absence of seeds, sprouts and stalks do not arise; therefore, it is said that those aggregates, bases, and elements are likewise free from grasping and abandoning.
How is it that the bodhicitta is without grasping and without relinquishing?
As the Buddha has said, he addressed the Lord of Secrets:

"Regarding that bodhicitta, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, understands that mind to be neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white, neither crimson nor crystal-colored; it is neither short nor long, neither round nor square, neither bright nor dark, and neither female, male, nor neuter."
Furthermore, Lord of Mysteries!

The bodhicitta is not of the nature of the desire realm, nor of the form realm, nor of the formless realm; it is not of the nature of yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, or non-humans, and so forth, up to and including the seeking of omniscience—it cannot be found.
Since such a grasping mind does not exist, how can one speak of its relinquishment?
Furthermore, as the Buddha said, he addressed Guhyapati:
"The bodhicitta is neither internal, nor external, nor in between, because it cannot be apprehended."
What do you think?
It is because its intrinsic nature is quiescent.
Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets!
That bodhicitta cannot be found when sought through omniscience; how, then, could it be grasped or abandoned?
Thus, regarding all phenomena, one attains freedom from grasping and abandoning, which is equality and selflessness.
As all phenomena are, so too is non-self.
As the Buddha has taught, so too is the bodhicitta.
All phenomena are empty, signless, and selfless; all phenomena are quiescent, yet they possess no characteristic of quiescence.
The mind is fundamentally equal; it is originally neither born nor unborn.
Furthermore, what is its nature? He replied:
Emptiness. What is the nature of emptiness?
It is because it is like space.
As the Buddha has taught, the nature of space is empty and beyond analogy;
the bodhicitta is likewise. The name "bodhi" is neither a nature nor a characteristic; it is without arising and without cessation, neither awakening nor non-awakening.
If one understands in this way, it is called the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said, he addressed Guhyapati:
"To understand one's own fundamental mind as it truly is, and to find that even non-existent phenomena are unobtainable—for this reason, it is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Again, he addressed the Lord of Secrets:

"Having first contemplated your own mind as it truly is, you should then initiate skillful means to contemplate sentient beings. You should know that all sentient beings do not understand the nature of their own self-awakening as it truly is; they give rise to doubt, delusion, inversion, and attachment, thereby undergoing the various great sufferings of saṃsāra."
On this account, I give rise to great compassion, causing all sentient beings to realize and awaken to the phenomena of their own minds as they truly are.
This is precisely what is called the bodhicitta; it is called the mind of benefit, the mind of peace and happiness, the supreme mind, and the mind of excellent awakening within the dharmadhātu.
Because it gathers all sentient beings through such wisdom, it is called the bodhicitta.
Since one gives rise to this mind, the merit obtained is likewise as boundless as space; the ocean of its merit is also immeasurable, remaining inexhaustible even when the kalpa comes to an end.
This is called the supreme bodhicitta, which is the root of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
*Bodhicittabhāvanāṭīkā*, one fascicle.
